strengths: The paper presents a useful contribution: conditioning scene-coordinate prediction on a compact collection of features from multiple posed reference images, enabling localization without scene-specific training or 3D reconstruction.

Evaluation across five benchmarks provides concrete evidence of competitiveness. FastForward reduces Cambridge's average median translation error from Reloc3r's 0.52 m to 0.27 m, improves Indoor6 accuracy at 10 cm/10° from 57.4% to 91.1%, and substantially reduces catastrophic translation errors on Wayspots.

The comparisons cover relative-pose regression, scene-coordinate regression, and structure-based localization. Shared retrieval settings for the principal feed-forward competitors improve comparability, and the appendix examines alternative MASt3R pose-estimation strategies.

The fixed-feature-budget experiment supports the value of aggregating multiple reference views. Additional experiments investigate feature count, retrieval-free reference selection, and generalization beyond the training-time number of views.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded: removing normalization also removes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS from training. Consequently, Table 8 cannot isolate normalization's contribution, particularly to outdoor generalization. Both variants should also be compared using identical training data.

The efficiency claims require more complete accounting. The reported mapping times primarily measure retrieval-index construction, while reference-feature extraction is performed during localization. Appendix C.3 reports approximately 0.6 seconds for coordinate prediction plus 2.2 seconds for PnP-RANSAC in the outdoor configuration. Thus, complete localization is neither a single neural forward pass nor real-time. Matched end-to-end latency, peak memory, and cached versus uncached measurements would better establish the practical advantage.

The strongest representation claim exceeds the demonstrated scope. Main benchmark results use 1,500–3,000 reference features selected separately for each query through retrieval, whereas the evidence for only a few hundred features comes from one validation benchmark and weakens at the tighter angular threshold. This is a compact query-conditioned representation, not evidence that a few hundred stored features suffice for an entire scene.

Attribution to the proposed architecture remains incomplete. There are no controlled ablations of ray encoding or auxiliary mapping supervision, despite claims about their benefits. A baseline that explicitly uses known reference poses to recover scale or triangulate query correspondences would also clarify how much improvement comes from geometric conditioning versus the learned sparse aggregation.

Some geometric details need correction or clarification. Under the stated camera-to-scene pose convention, the viewing ray should use R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T, whereas Section 3.1 specifies (K R)^{-1}[u,v,1]^T. The scale definition also becomes zero for a single reference camera, although single-reference results are shown. These may be documentation issues, but the implementation conventions and degenerate-case handling are necessary for reproduction.

The conclusions overstate superiority to scene-coordinate regression. On 7-Scenes, FastForward reaches 73.2% at 5 cm/5° versus ACE's 97.1%; on Cambridge it remains behind the strongest structure-based methods. The evidence supports an attractive preparation-time/accuracy tradeoff rather than uniformly better localization.

strengths: The method offers a meaningful practical contribution: jointly conditioning scene-coordinate prediction on sampled features from multiple posed reference images, without scene-specific training or explicit scene reconstruction.

The evaluation provides concrete evidence of substantial improvements over Reloc3r across five datasets. Average median translation error decreases from 0.52 m to 0.27 m on Cambridge and from 1.31 m to 0.17 m on Wayspots; Indoor6 accuracy at 10 cm/10° increases from 57.4% to 91.1%.

Comparisons cover relevant alternatives, including scene-coordinate regression, structure-based localization, and feed-forward methods. The appendix additionally examines several MASt3R pose-estimation strategies.

The fixed-token-budget experiments support the value of incorporating multiple reference views. Training details, retrieval alternatives, and runtime measurements provide useful implementation and practical context.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded: the unnormalized model also excludes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS from training. Consequently, Table 8 cannot isolate normalization from changes in training diversity, particularly for the large Cambridge improvement. A comparison using identical training data is needed.

Efficiency claims need more careful qualification. Appendix C.3 reports 0.6 seconds for coordinate prediction plus 2.2 seconds for PnP on Wayspots. Constant decoder input size does not make total runtime independent of reference-image count, because all selected images are encoded. A matched end-to-end comparison with Reloc3r, including retrieval, encoding, pose solving, caching, and memory, is missing.

The contribution largely combines established DUSt3R components, ray conditioning, sampling, and previously used normalization. Ablations do not isolate ray encoding or mapping-head supervision, and there is no controlled comparison against a multi-view alternative using the same backbone and training data.

Claims of superiority over SCR and structure-based methods are broader than the results justify. Cambridge structure-based methods remain substantially more accurate; on 7-Scenes, ACE achieves 97.1% at 5 cm/5° versus 73.2% for FastForward. Wayspots improves average median error dramatically but does not surpass ACE or GLACE at 10 cm/10°. The contribution is best supported as an accuracy–preparation-time tradeoff.

Some reproducibility and robustness details remain unresolved. Scale normalization is undefined for a single reference camera or coincident camera centers, despite single-view examples. The ray-direction equation appears inconsistent with the stated camera-to-scene rotation convention. Random feature sampling is evaluated without variability estimates, and sensitivity to noisy mapping poses is not measured.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to generalizable visual localization: a fixed-size collection of features from multiple posed reference images enables joint query-coordinate prediction without scene-specific training or explicit scene reconstruction.

The improvements over Reloc3r are substantial across diverse benchmarks. Average median translation error decreases from 0.52m to 0.27m on Cambridge and from 1.31m to 0.17m on Wayspots; Indoor6 accuracy at 10cm/10° increases from 57.4% to 91.1%. These results provide concrete evidence of practical value.

Evaluation spans five indoor and outdoor datasets, including changing environments in RIO10. Comparisons include strong relative-pose, scene-coordinate, and structure-based methods, and the appendix investigates several MASt3R pose-estimation variants.

The feature-count and reference-image ablations support the central representation choice: incorporating more views improves accuracy even with a fixed token budget. Training details and additional per-scene results make the empirical contribution reasonably assessable.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded. The unnormalized model also removes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS from training, so Table 8 cannot isolate normalization from additional training data. This particularly weakens the claimed explanation for the large Cambridge improvement; a matched-data comparison is needed.

The efficiency claims need tighter qualification. Appendix C.3 reports 0.6 seconds for coordinate prediction plus 2.2 seconds for PnP-RANSAC on Wayspots. Thus, the complete localization pipeline is neither a single neural forward pass nor real-time. The reported mapping times count retrieval preparation while reference-feature extraction is paid during inference; fixed decoder token count does not imply constant total runtime as reference-image count grows. Comparable end-to-end latency, caching, and memory measurements are missing.

The architectural novelty is primarily the adaptation of DUSt3R to sampled, pose-conditioned multi-image features. The paper cites recent multi-view geometry models but does not experimentally establish its advantage over an appropriate multi-view baseline. Ablations of ray conditioning and auxiliary mapping-head supervision would also strengthen attribution of the gains.

Several superiority claims are broader than the results. On Wayspots, 10cm/10° accuracy is 51.0%, below ACE's 51.9% and GLACE's 52.4%, despite substantially improved average median translation error. On 7-Scenes, accuracy at 5cm/5° is 73.2%, versus ACE's 97.1%; Cambridge structure-based methods also remain considerably more accurate. The contribution is a favorable preparation-time/accuracy tradeoff rather than uniformly superior localization.

Some reproducibility and robustness details remain unresolved: no variation across random feature samples is reported, pose-solver settings are incomplete, and the normalization formula gives zero scale for a single reference image even though single-image results are shown. Sensitivity to noisy mapping poses would also be valuable given the proposed use with tracked camera poses.

strengths: The method offers a useful contribution: jointly processing a fixed-size collection of pose-conditioned mapping features to predict query scene coordinates, without scene-specific training or explicit map triangulation.

The evaluation spans five diverse benchmarks and demonstrates concrete benefits. On Wayspots, the average scene-median translation error improves from 0.51 m for E5+1 to 0.17 m; on Indoor6, accuracy at 10 cm/10° reaches 91.5%, exceeding all reported competitors.

The accuracy–runtime trade-off is compelling for on-demand localization: approximately 0.3–0.5 seconds per query with seconds of retrieval-index preparation. Comparisons include both learned and geometric methods, generally using identical retrieved reference images.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, feature-budget and reference-count experiments, retrieval-free variants, and alternative configurations for MASt3R and E5+1. These analyses strengthen the practical contribution.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded. Appendix C.1 removes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS when disabling normalization, changing both the method and training data. Consequently, the large Cambridge improvement cannot be attributed specifically to normalization. A comparison using identical training data is needed.

The architectural novelty is relatively focused: the backbone, decoder, prediction head, and confidence loss largely follow DUSt3R, while scale normalization follows prior work. Controlled ablations of ray conditioning and auxiliary mapping supervision, plus comparison with a straightforward multi-view adaptation, would better establish which design choices drive the gains.

Some headline claims exceed the results. FastForward trails E5+1 on Cambridge, MASt3R at the stricter RIO10 threshold, and SCR methods substantially on 7-Scenes. The conclusion claiming higher indoor accuracy than SCR is therefore too broad; the evidence supports a useful trade-off rather than general superiority.

The compact-map and constant-runtime claims need qualification. Main benchmark configurations use 1,500–3,000 mapping tokens, retain mapping images for retrieval, and recompute their encoder features. Appendix C.3 acknowledges that total runtime grows with reference-image count. Fixed decoder input size does not establish constant end-to-end runtime or compact total storage, and measured memory/storage comparisons are missing.

There are technical specification gaps. Under the stated camera-to-scene pose convention, the ray direction should use R K^{-1}, whereas Section 3.1 gives (K R)^{-1}. Scale normalization is also undefined for a single reference camera after centering, despite single-reference examples and ablations. These may be documentation issues, but require clarification. Random feature sampling and RANSAC results additionally lack repeated-run variability.

strengths: FastForward offers a useful contribution: jointly processing sampled features from multiple posed mapping images to predict query scene coordinates, avoiding scene-specific training and explicit map triangulation. The resulting accuracy–preparation-time trade-off is practically meaningful.

The strongest results are substantial. On Wayspots, the average per-scene median translation error falls from 0.51 m for E5+1 with ALIKED-LightGlue to 0.17 m. On Indoor6, accuracy at 10 cm/10° reaches 91.5%, compared with 80.9% for E5+1 and 89.0% for MASt3R+Kapture.

Evaluation spans five benchmarks and includes geometric, relative-pose, scene-coordinate, and structure-based approaches. Shared retrieval candidates improve comparison fairness, and the appendix explores alternative MASt3R solvers and E5+1 accuracy–latency configurations.

The fixed-token multi-view experiments support the value of incorporating additional views. Training settings, computational resources, inference procedures, and exclusion of Wayspots scenes from task-specific training are described in useful detail.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded: the unnormalized model also excludes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS from training (Appendix C.1). Consequently, the large Cambridge improvement cannot be attributed specifically to normalization. A comparison using identical training data is needed to establish this central claim.

The architectural novelty is primarily an effective combination of existing components: DUSt3R initialization and decoding, Fourier ray encodings, coordinate normalization, and random token sampling. Missing ablations for ray encoding, auxiliary mapping supervision, and alternative token-selection strategies limit understanding of which changes drive the gains.

The compact-map and constant-runtime claims require qualification. Standard evaluations use 1,500–3,000 mapping tokens and retain mapping images and retrieval descriptors; a few hundred tokens are examined only on Map-free validation. Fixed token count bounds decoder computation, while Appendix C.3 explicitly acknowledges that image-encoding cost grows with the number of mapping views. Quantitative storage and peak-memory comparisons are missing.

Performance leadership is conditional. E5+1 is more accurate on Cambridge (0.18 m versus 0.27 m), MASt3R leads at the tighter RIO10 threshold, and ACE substantially outperforms FastForward on 7-Scenes. The conclusion's broad claims of superiority over SCR on indoor datasets and comparable outdoor performance should be narrowed.

Random feature sampling and correspondence subsampling are evaluated without repeated-run variability. This matters for smaller improvements, such as 51.4% versus 49.5% on Wayspots. Controlled tests of mapping-pose noise, retrieval failures, and larger mapping collections would also strengthen the robustness and scalability claims.

strengths: FastForward makes a useful contribution to localization without scene-specific training: jointly processing sampled features from multiple posed reference images enables direct scene-coordinate prediction and avoids pairwise pose aggregation.

The evaluation spans five indoor and outdoor benchmarks with relevant SCR, relative-pose, matching-based, and structure-based competitors. Shared retrieval candidates improve fairness, and the appendix investigates alternative MASt3R solvers and E5+1 accuracy–latency trade-offs.

There is concrete evidence of a competitive accuracy–efficiency trade-off. On Wayspots, the average scene-median translation error falls from 0.51 m for E5+1 with ALIKED-LightGlue to 0.17 m. On Indoor6, FastForward reaches 91.5% accuracy at 10 cm/10°, compared with 80.9% for that baseline and 89.0% for MASt3R+Kapture.

Mapping preparation takes seconds, with reported query latency of 0.3–0.5 seconds. Feature-count and reference-view ablations support the usefulness of compact multi-view representations, and training details and practical limitations are reasonably well documented.
weaknesses: The scale-normalization ablation is confounded: removing normalization also removes MegaDepth and BlendedMVS from training. Consequently, Table 8 cannot isolate normalization from training-data diversity, particularly for the large Cambridge improvement. A matched-data comparison is needed to substantiate this central attribution.

The main benchmark results use 1,500–3,000 mapping features, whereas the headline claim emphasizes only a few hundred. Evidence for very small representations comes primarily from Map-free validation. The paper should demonstrate the same accuracy–latency trade-off across its principal test benchmarks and quantify variability from random feature sampling.

Some conclusions overstate the scope of the gains. E5+1 is more accurate on Cambridge (0.18 m versus 0.27 m), ACE substantially outperforms FastForward on 7-Scenes, and MASt3R leads at the tighter RIO10 threshold. The evidence supports a useful operating point rather than general superiority over SCR or structure-based localization.

The compact representation bounds decoder input size, not total map storage or end-to-end computation. The retrieval database still retains mapping images, and reference-image encoding scales with the number of selected views. More complete memory measurements and cached versus uncached latency comparisons would strengthen the efficiency claims.

Several technical details need clarification. Under the stated camera-to-scene rotation convention, the ray-direction formula appears inconsistent with the expected R K^{-1} transformation. Scale normalization is undefined for a single reference view or coincident camera centers, despite single-view examples. The auxiliary mapping-head benefit is also asserted without a controlled ablation.
